decks.title: Human Reproduction — Part 1: The male and female reproductive systems
goals: Label the male reproductive system and trace the path of sperms
State the roles of the testes, ducts and accessory glands
Label the female reproductive system, including the parts of the oviduct and the uterine wall

slides.heading: Human Reproduction
slides.body_md: Part 1 — humans reproduce sexually and are viviparous. We begin with the organs that make gametes and support the young.

visual.alt: Flow of the main events of human reproduction from gametogenesis to parturition

slides.narration: Humans reproduce sexually and give birth to live young, so we are called viviparous. The process has a clear sequence: making gametes, transferring sperms, fertilisation, implantation of the embryo, development in the uterus, and birth. In this part we study the organs involved, using simple labelled diagrams.

slides.heading: Events of human reproduction
slides.body_md: Reproductive events begin at **puberty**. There are clear differences between males and females: for example, sperm formation continues into old age, but egg formation in women stops at about 50 years.

rows: Formation of sperms in males and ova in females
Transfer of sperms into the female genital tract
Fusion of a sperm and an ovum, forming a zygote
The blastocyst attaches to the uterine wall
Development of the embryo and foetus in the uterus

visual.alt: Table of the six events of human reproduction with what happens in each

slides.narration: Here are six words you will meet again and again. Gametogenesis makes the gametes. Insemination transfers sperms into the female tract. Fertilisation fuses sperm and ovum. Implantation attaches the young embryo to the uterus. Gestation is the period of development, and parturition is birth. Keep this list as a map for the whole chapter.

slides.heading: The male reproductive system
slides.body_md: It lies in the pelvis and has a pair of **testes**, **accessory ducts**, **accessory glands** and the **external genitalia**. The testes sit outside the abdominal cavity in a pouch called the **scrotum**.

slides.narration: Let us read the diagram from bottom to top. Each testis lies in the scrotum, with a coiled epididymis along its side. A vas deferens runs up from each side, loops over the bladder and, joined by the duct of the seminal vesicle, forms an ejaculatory duct that opens into the urethra. The prostate and bulbourethral glands add their secretions along the way.

slides.heading: Inside the testis
slides.body_md: The scrotum keeps the testes about **2–2.5 °C below** body temperature, which sperm formation needs. Each testis has about **250 compartments** called **testicular lobules**, each with **one to three** highly coiled **seminiferous tubules**.

rows: Immunologically competent cells; blood vessels nearby

visual.alt: Table of cells of the testis: spermatogonia, Sertoli cells and interstitial cells, with where they lie and their roles

slides.narration: The testis is a factory with two departments. Inside the seminiferous tubules, germ cells are turned into sperms, helped and fed by the Sertoli cells. In the spaces between the tubules, the interstitial or Leydig cells make male hormones called androgens. The scrotum keeps the factory a little cooler than the rest of the body, which sperm production requires.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how many seminiferous tubules?
slides.body_md: A testis has about 250 lobules, each with one to three seminiferous tubules. What is the possible range of tubules in one testis, and in both testes together?
bullets: Step 1 — Fewest tubules in one testis: $250 \times 1 = 250$.
Step 2 — Most tubules in one testis: $250 \times 3 = 750$.
Step 3 — Two testes: from $2 \times 250 = 500$ to $2 \times 750 = 1500$.
Conclusion — hundreds of tightly coiled tubules give a huge surface for sperm production.

visual.alt: Worked table: 250 to 750 tubules in one testis and 500 to 1500 in both

slides.narration: Multiply the number of lobules by the smallest and largest number of tubules in each. One testis has between two hundred and fifty and seven hundred and fifty tubules; two testes have between five hundred and fifteen hundred. All of them are tightly coiled, so a huge length of tubule fits in a small organ.

slides.heading: The duct system
slides.body_md: Sperms leave the testis through a chain of ducts and reach the outside through the **urethra**, which opens at the **urethral meatus**.

edges.label: joined by the seminal vesicle duct

visual.alt: Flow of the male duct system from the seminiferous tubules to the urethral meatus

slides.narration: Memorise this route as a chain. Seminiferous tubules open into the rete testis, then the vasa efferentia lead into the epididymis on the back of the testis. The vas deferens carries sperms up into the abdomen, joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct, and this opens into the urethra, which carries sperms to the outside.

slides.heading: Quick check: the order of the ducts
slides.body_md: Which sequence shows the correct path of sperms?
slides.narration: Quick check. Start inside the testis and move outwards one duct at a time.

slides.heading: Accessory glands and semen
slides.body_md: The secretions of the accessory glands form the **seminal plasma**, which is rich in **fructose, calcium** and certain **enzymes**. Sperms together with seminal plasma make up **semen**.

rows: Part of seminal plasma (fructose is an energy source for sperms)
Secretion that helps lubricate the penis

visual.alt: Table of the male accessory glands, their number and their contributions

slides.narration: Sperms cannot travel or survive on their own. The seminal vesicles, the prostate and the bulbourethral glands add fluids that carry them and feed them. Fructose in seminal plasma is the fuel for the sperm’s swimming. The penis is the external organ, with a sensitive tip called the glans penis covered by the foreskin.

slides.heading: The female reproductive system
slides.body_md: It has a pair of **ovaries**, a pair of **oviducts**, the **uterus**, the **cervix**, the **vagina** and the external genitalia, together with a pair of **mammary glands**.

slides.narration: Each ovary lies close to the funnel-shaped end of an oviduct. The oviduct leads into the uterus, a hollow muscular organ shaped like an inverted pear. The narrow lower part of the uterus is the cervix, which opens into the vagina. The cervical canal and the vagina together form the birth canal.

slides.heading: Ovaries and oviducts
slides.body_md: The **ovaries** are the primary female sex organs; they produce the **ovum** and **ovarian hormones**. Each **oviduct** (fallopian tube) has three parts.

rows: About 2–4 cm long; connected to the pelvic wall and uterus by ligaments; stroma has an outer cortex and an inner medulla
Funnel-shaped part near the ovary, with finger-like fimbriae that help collect the ovum after ovulation
Last, narrow part that joins the uterus

visual.alt: Table of key facts about the ovary and the three parts of the oviduct

slides.narration: The ovary is small, only two to four centimetres long, but it does two jobs: it releases the ovum and makes hormones. The oviduct starts as the infundibulum, a funnel with finger-like fimbriae that sweep the released ovum inside. Then comes the wider ampulla and finally the narrow isthmus, which joins the uterus.

slides.heading: The uterus and its wall
slides.body_md: The **uterus** (womb) is single, shaped like an inverted pear, and held by ligaments to the pelvic wall. Its wall has **three layers**.

rows: Thick middle layer of smooth muscle
Strong contractions during delivery of the baby
Inner glandular layer lining the cavity
Changes in every menstrual cycle; receives the embryo

visual.alt: Table of the three layers of the uterine wall with their description and role

slides.narration: Remember the layers from outside in: perimetrium, myometrium, endometrium. The myometrium is thick smooth muscle, and it produces the powerful contractions of childbirth. The endometrium is the living inner lining. It thickens and breaks down in each menstrual cycle, and it is where the embryo implants if fertilisation happens.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: where does each event happen?
slides.body_md: Name the part of the female reproductive system where each event takes place.
bullets: Release of the secondary oocyte → **ovary** (ovulation).
Collection of the oocyte → **infundibulum**, helped by the fimbriae.
Fertilisation → **ampulla** (the ampullary–isthmic junction).
Implantation of the blastocyst → **endometrium** of the uterus.
Passage of the baby at birth → **cervical canal and vagina** (birth canal).

visual.alt: Worked table of five events and where each takes place in the female reproductive system

slides.narration: Location questions are common and easy to lose marks on. Fertilisation happens in the oviduct, in the ampulla region, not in the uterus. The uterus is where the young embryo implants and grows. And the cervical canal together with the vagina forms the birth canal through which the baby passes.

slides.heading: Quick check: which layer pushes?
slides.body_md: Which layer of the uterine wall produces strong contractions during the delivery of a baby?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about which layer is made of muscle.

slides.heading: External genitalia and mammary glands
slides.body_md: The female external genitalia include the **mons pubis**, **labia majora**, **labia minora**, **hymen** and **clitoris**. The hymen may be torn by many everyday activities, so its presence or absence is **not** a reliable indicator of anything. The **mammary glands** are paired structures that contain glandular tissue and fat.

visual.alt: Flow of milk from alveoli through mammary tubules, ducts and ampulla to the lactiferous duct

slides.narration: Each mammary gland has fifteen to twenty mammary lobes, with clusters of cells called alveoli that secrete milk. Milk is stored in the cavities of the alveoli, then flows through mammary tubules into ducts, which join to form a wider mammary ampulla connected to the lactiferous duct, through which the baby sucks out milk.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Testes in the scrotum (2–2.5 °C cooler); about 250 lobules, each with 1–3 seminiferous tubules; spermatogonia and Sertoli cells inside, Leydig cells (androgens) outside.
Ducts: rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra → urethral meatus.
Accessory glands: seminal vesicles, prostate, bulbourethral glands; seminal plasma rich in fructose, calcium and enzymes.
Ovary (2–4 cm); oviduct: infundibulum with fimbriae, ampulla, isthmus; uterus: perimetrium, myometrium, endometrium; cervix + vagina = birth canal.
Mammary gland: alveoli → tubules → duct → ampulla → lactiferous duct.

visual.alt: Summary table comparing the male and female systems

slides.narration: Let us recap. In males, testes make sperms and androgens, ducts carry the sperms, and glands add seminal plasma. In females, ovaries release the ovum and make hormones, the oviduct collects it, the uterus houses the embryo, and the mammary glands later feed the baby. Next, we look inside the testis and ovary at how gametes are made.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Draw both systems as **front-view schematics** with neat label lines; examiners want the parts, not artistic detail.
Write the male duct sequence in the **correct order** — a common 2-mark question.
Name all **three parts of the oviduct** and **three layers of the uterus**.
Fertilisation is in the **ampulla**, implantation in the **endometrium**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Practise both diagrams until you can label them quickly. Learn the duct sequence as a chain without gaps. Name all three parts of the oviduct and all three layers of the uterine wall, and never write that fertilisation happens in the uterus.

goals: Describe spermatogenesis and its hormonal control, and the structure of a sperm

slides.heading: Gametogenesis and the menstrual cycle
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how the testis makes sperms, how the ovary prepares an ovum, and how the uterus prepares every month for a possible pregnancy.

visual.alt: Flow showing hormones controlling spermatogenesis, oogenesis and the menstrual cycle

slides.narration: Gametes are made by gametogenesis: spermatogenesis in the testis and oogenesis in the ovary. Both use meiosis, so the gametes are haploid. Both are controlled by hormones from the pituitary gland and the gonads. In women these hormones also drive a monthly cycle in the ovary and uterus, called the menstrual cycle.

slides.heading: Inside a seminiferous tubule
slides.body_md: Sperm production runs from the **wall** of the tubule towards the **lumen**: spermatogonia at the wall, then spermatocytes and spermatids, and sperms released into the lumen. **Sertoli cells** support them; **Leydig cells** lie outside.

slides.heading: Spermatogenesis
slides.body_md: Spermatogenesis begins at **puberty**. Diploid **spermatogonia** multiply by mitosis; some become **primary spermatocytes**, which undergo **meiosis**.

visual.alt: Flow of spermatogenesis from spermatogonium through primary and secondary spermatocytes and spermatids to sperms, with chromosome numbers

slides.narration: Follow the chromosome numbers. A spermatogonium and a primary spermatocyte both have forty-six. The first meiotic division gives two secondary spermatocytes with twenty-three each. The second division gives four spermatids, still with twenty-three. The spermatids are then remodelled into sperms; this is spermiogenesis. Finally, sperms are released into the lumen; this release is spermiation.

slides.heading: Hormones that drive spermatogenesis
slides.body_md: At puberty, the **hypothalamus** increases its secretion of **GnRH**, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release two **gonadotropins**.

visual.alt: Flow of hormonal control: GnRH acts on the pituitary; LH acts on Leydig cells to release androgens; FSH acts on Sertoli cells

slides.narration: Two pituitary hormones share the work. Luteinising hormone acts on the Leydig cells, which respond by making androgens, and androgens stimulate sperm production. Follicle stimulating hormone acts on the Sertoli cells and helps them release factors needed for spermiogenesis. Both are switched on by gonadotropin releasing hormone from the hypothalamus at puberty.

slides.heading: Structure of a sperm
slides.body_md: A sperm is a microscopic structure with a **head**, **neck**, **middle piece** and **tail**, covered by a plasma membrane. The head holds the haploid **nucleus** and a cap-like **acrosome** filled with enzymes that help it penetrate the ovum. The middle piece has many **mitochondria**, which supply energy for the tail to move.

slides.narration: Each part of the sperm has one clear job. The acrosome carries enzymes to get through the layers around the ovum. The nucleus carries the father’s chromosomes. The middle piece is the power station, full of mitochondria. And the tail lashes to move the sperm, which is essential for it to reach the ovum.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting gametes and chromosomes
slides.body_md: A sample of testis tissue contains 50 primary spermatocytes, all completing meiosis. How many secondary spermatocytes, spermatids and sperms will form, and how many chromosomes does each type of cell carry?
bullets: Step 1 — Meiosis I: each primary spermatocyte gives 2 secondary spermatocytes: $50 \times 2 = 100$.
Step 2 — Meiosis II: each secondary spermatocyte gives 2 spermatids: $100 \times 2 = 200$.
Step 3 — Each spermatid becomes one sperm: **200 sperms**.
Chromosomes — primary spermatocyte 46; secondary spermatocyte, spermatid and sperm 23 each.

visual.alt: Worked table: 50 primary spermatocytes give 100 secondary spermatocytes, 200 spermatids and 200 sperms

slides.narration: Each meiotic division doubles the number of cells, so fifty primary spermatocytes give one hundred secondary spermatocytes and then two hundred spermatids, which become two hundred sperms. The chromosome number halves at the first meiotic division, from forty-six to twenty-three, and then stays at twenty-three. Compare this with oogenesis next: fifty primary oocytes give only fifty ova.

slides.heading: Oogenesis begins before birth
slides.body_md: Oogenesis starts during **embryonic development**. Millions of **oogonia** form in each foetal ovary; **no more** are added after birth. They start meiosis and stop at prophase of the first division as **primary oocytes**.

nodes.label: About 60 000 to 80 000 per ovary at puberty

visual.alt: Flow of early oogenesis from oogonia in the foetal ovary to primary follicles, with many degenerating before puberty

slides.narration: This is a striking difference from males. A baby girl is born with all the egg-forming cells she will ever have, already started on meiosis and paused. Each primary oocyte gets wrapped in a layer of granulosa cells, forming a primary follicle. Many follicles die away during childhood, leaving roughly sixty to eighty thousand in each ovary at puberty.

slides.heading: Follicles in the ovary
slides.body_md: Primary follicles gain more layers of granulosa cells and a new **theca**, becoming **secondary follicles**. A fluid-filled cavity, the **antrum**, then forms in the **tertiary follicle**, which grows into a mature **Graafian follicle**.

visual.caption: Schematic: all stages drawn in one ovary for comparison.

slides.narration: In this drawing all the stages are shown together so you can compare them. The primary follicle has one layer of cells around the oocyte. The secondary follicle has many layers. The tertiary follicle has a fluid-filled space called the antrum. The mature Graafian follicle bursts at ovulation, and what remains becomes the corpus luteum.

slides.heading: Completing meiosis: oocyte and polar bodies
slides.body_md: In the tertiary follicle, the primary oocyte **completes meiosis I** with an **unequal** division: a large haploid **secondary oocyte** and a tiny **first polar body**. The secondary oocyte keeps most of the nutrient-rich cytoplasm and forms a new membrane, the **zona pellucida**. At **ovulation**, the Graafian follicle ruptures and releases the secondary oocyte.

nodes.label: Meiosis II completed only after a sperm enters

visual.alt: Flow of later oogenesis: unequal meiosis I, Graafian follicle, ovulation, and completion of meiosis II after sperm entry

slides.narration: Why is the division unequal? The future ovum must carry enough cytoplasm and food for the embryo’s first days, so almost all of it stays in one cell. The small polar body gets just a set of chromosomes. Note that what leaves the ovary at ovulation is a secondary oocyte; its second meiotic division is completed only when a sperm enters it.

slides.heading: Spermatogenesis and oogenesis compared
slides.body_md: Both make haploid gametes by meiosis, but the timing and output are very different.

rows: One ovum; the rest go into polar bodies
Secondary oocyte, about one per cycle

visual.alt: Table comparing spermatogenesis and oogenesis by start, duration, output, divisions and the gamete released

slides.narration: Put the two side by side. Sperm production starts at puberty and continues for life, and each primary spermatocyte gives four sperms. Egg production starts before birth, pauses for years, and each primary oocyte yields just one ovum, with the other products being small polar bodies. Usually only one secondary oocyte is released per menstrual cycle.

slides.heading: The menstrual cycle
slides.body_md: The reproductive cycle of female primates is the **menstrual cycle**. The first one, at puberty, is **menarche**. In women it repeats roughly every **28 or 29 days** and stops at about 50 years (**menopause**). One ovum is usually released in the middle of each cycle.

rows: Endometrium and its blood vessels break down and flow out
LH surge; Graafian follicle releases the secondary oocyte
Corpus luteum secretes progesterone; endometrium maintained

visual.alt: Table of the four phases of a 28-day menstrual cycle with days and main events

slides.narration: The cycle is counted from the first day of menstrual flow. For about three to five days the endometrium breaks down and flows out. Then follicles grow and the lining rebuilds. Around day fourteen an ovum is released. For the rest of the cycle the corpus luteum keeps the lining ready. If no pregnancy follows, the cycle starts again.

slides.heading: Hormones across the cycle
slides.body_md: Pituitary hormones (**LH, FSH**) and ovarian hormones (**estrogen, progesterone**) rise and fall in a coordinated pattern. The diagram is qualitative.

slides.narration: Read the diagram from left to right. In the follicular phase, estrogen from the growing follicles rises. Near the middle, LH and FSH reach their peak; the sharp LH surge triggers ovulation. Afterwards, progesterone from the corpus luteum climbs and stays high. At the end, progesterone falls, and the endometrium breaks down again.

slides.heading: What controls each phase
slides.body_md: The **corpus luteum** is the key to the second half of the cycle.

nodes.label: LH and FSH rise: follicles grow, estrogen rises
Corpus luteum: progesterone maintains the endometrium
No fertilisation: corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls
Fertilisation: corpus luteum stays, no menstruation

visual.alt: Flow of hormonal control: follicle growth and estrogen, LH surge and ovulation, corpus luteum and progesterone, then menstruation or pregnancy

slides.narration: Progesterone is the hormone that keeps the endometrium ready for implantation. It comes from the corpus luteum. If no fertilisation happens, the corpus luteum breaks down, progesterone falls and the lining is shed. If fertilisation does happen, the corpus luteum is maintained, so menstruation stops. That is why missed periods can be a sign of pregnancy, though stress and poor health can also cause them.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reading a 28-day cycle
slides.body_md: In a regular 28-day cycle, name the phase, a hormone that is high, and the state of the endometrium on days 3, 10, 14 and 22.
bullets: Day 3 → **menstrual** phase; progesterone has fallen; the endometrium is breaking down.
Day 10 → **follicular** phase; **estrogen** rising from growing follicles; the endometrium is regenerating.
Day 14 → **ovulation**; **LH** at its peak (with FSH); the endometrium is thick.
Day 22 → **luteal** phase; **progesterone** high from the corpus luteum; the endometrium is maintained and glandular.

visual.alt: Worked table of phase, high hormone and endometrium state on days 3, 10, 14 and 22 of a 28-day cycle

slides.narration: For each day, first find the phase, then ask which gland is most active. In the follicular phase it is the growing follicles, making estrogen. At mid-cycle, the pituitary releases its LH surge. In the luteal phase it is the corpus luteum, making progesterone. The state of the endometrium follows from these hormones.

slides.narration: Quick check. Recall what the corpus luteum makes and what that hormone does.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Spermatogenesis: spermatogonium → primary spermatocyte (46) → two secondary spermatocytes (23) → four spermatids → four sperms (spermiogenesis); release = spermiation.
GnRH → LH (Leydig cells → androgens) and FSH (Sertoli cells → spermiogenesis factors).
Sperm: acrosome + nucleus (head), neck, middle piece (mitochondria), tail.

Oogenesis starts before birth; primary oocytes pause in meiosis I; follicles: primary → secondary → tertiary (antrum) → Graafian; unequal division gives secondary oocyte + polar body; ovulation releases the secondary oocyte.
Menstrual cycle (about 28 days): menstrual, follicular, ovulation (LH surge), luteal (progesterone from the corpus luteum).

rows: Follicle growth; LH surge causes ovulation

visual.alt: Summary table of the hormones of the menstrual cycle with source and role

slides.narration: To recap: sperms are made continuously from puberty, four from each primary spermatocyte. Ova are prepared from cells formed before birth, one at a time, with polar bodies taking the spare chromosomes. The menstrual cycle links the ovary and uterus through hormones, with the LH surge causing ovulation and progesterone keeping the lining ready.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Draw spermatogenesis and oogenesis as **flow charts with ploidy** (46 or 23) at each stage.
Say that the gamete released at ovulation is a **secondary oocyte**.
Name the **LH surge** as the cause of ovulation and the **corpus luteum** as the source of progesterone.
Do not call the follicular phase "secretory"; it is **proliferative**. The luteal phase is **secretory**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Write chromosome numbers on every arrow of your gametogenesis charts. Say secondary oocyte, not mature ovum, for what is released at ovulation. Link the LH surge to ovulation and the corpus luteum to progesterone. And keep the two names straight: follicular is proliferative, luteal is secretory.

slides.heading: Fertilisation to birth
slides.body_md: Part 3 — from the meeting of sperm and ovum to the birth of a baby and breastfeeding.

visual.alt: Flow from fertilisation to cleavage, implantation, placenta and pregnancy, parturition and lactation

slides.narration: In this part we follow a single cell, the zygote, as it divides, travels down the oviduct, settles into the uterus and grows into a baby over about nine months. We will also see how the mother’s body prepares for birth and for feeding the newborn.

slides.heading: Fertilisation
slides.body_md: During **insemination**, sperms are released into the vagina. Motile sperms swim through the cervix and uterus into the oviduct. The ovum released from the ovary is also carried into the oviduct. **Fertilisation** can happen only if the ovum and sperms reach the **ampullary region** together.

nodes.label: Changes in the membrane block other sperms
Acrosome enzymes help the sperm enter
Secondary oocyte completes meiosis II: ovum + second polar body

visual.alt: Flow of fertilisation: sperm contact, block to other sperms, entry, completion of meiosis II and fusion to form the zygote

slides.narration: Only a few sperms reach the ampulla, and timing matters: this is why not every insemination leads to fertilisation. When a sperm contacts the zona pellucida, the membrane changes so that no other sperm can enter. The acrosome’s enzymes help the sperm in. Its entry triggers the oocyte to finish meiosis, and then the two haploid nuclei fuse into a diploid zygote.

slides.heading: Who decides the sex of the baby?
slides.body_md: Women have **XX** sex chromosomes and men **XY**. Every ovum carries an **X**. Half the sperms carry an **X** and half carry a **Y**. The sex of the baby is therefore decided by the **sperm**, that is, by the father.

visual.alt: Table showing that an X-bearing sperm gives a female zygote and a Y-bearing sperm gives a male zygote

slides.narration: All eggs carry an X chromosome, so the mother always passes on an X. The father’s sperm may carry an X or a Y. If an X-bearing sperm fertilises the ovum, the baby is a girl; if a Y-bearing sperm does, the baby is a boy. So it is scientifically wrong, and unjust, to blame a mother for the sex of her child.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: chance of a girl or a boy
slides.body_md: In each pregnancy, X-bearing and Y-bearing sperms are equally likely to fertilise the ovum. What is the probability that (a) the next baby is a girl, and (b) both of a couple’s two children are girls?
bullets: Step 1 — Half the sperms carry X, so P(girl) $= \dfrac{1}{2}$ in every pregnancy, whatever happened before.
Step 2 — Two independent pregnancies: P(both girls) $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.25$.
Conclusion — earlier births do not change the chance for the next one.

visual.alt: Worked table: each of the four orders of two children has probability one quarter

slides.narration: Each pregnancy is like a fresh coin toss decided by the sperm. The chance of a girl is one half every time, even if a family already has several girls. For two children, there are four equally likely orders, so the chance that both are girls is one quarter, the same as the chance that both are boys.

slides.narration: Cleavage divisions are fast and the embryo does not grow in size; it simply splits into smaller and smaller cells. By the time it reaches the uterus, it has become a solid ball called a morula. The morula keeps dividing and turns into a hollow ball, the blastocyst, which is the stage that implants.

slides.heading: The blastocyst and implantation
slides.body_md: In the **blastocyst**, the outer layer of cells is the **trophoblast** and the cells attached to it inside form the **inner cell mass**. The trophoblast attaches to the **endometrium**; the uterine cells divide rapidly and cover the blastocyst, which becomes embedded: **implantation**. The inner cell mass becomes the **embryo**.

slides.narration: Think of the blastocyst as having two teams. The trophoblast is the outer team that anchors the embryo to the uterus and helps form the placenta. The inner cell mass is the team that becomes the baby. After the trophoblast attaches, the endometrium grows over the blastocyst and it is fully embedded. Pregnancy has now begun.

slides.heading: Quick check: which part becomes the baby?
slides.body_md: Which part of the blastocyst develops into the embryo?
slides.narration: Quick check. One part attaches to the uterus; the other forms the body.

slides.heading: The placenta
slides.body_md: After implantation, finger-like **chorionic villi** grow from the trophoblast and interlock with uterine tissue, forming the **placenta**, a structural and functional unit between embryo and mother. It is joined to the embryo by the **umbilical cord**, which carries substances to and from the embryo.

rows: Oxygen and nutrients pass from the mother’s blood to the embryo
Carbon dioxide and excretory wastes pass from the embryo to the mother
Makes human chorionic gonadotropin, human placental lactogen, estrogens and progestogens

visual.alt: Table of the functions of the placenta: supply, removal and hormone production

slides.narration: The placenta is a remarkable shared organ. The mother’s blood and the baby’s blood come very close in the villi, close enough for oxygen and food to cross one way and carbon dioxide and wastes the other way. The umbilical cord is the cable connecting the placenta to the baby. The placenta also works as a hormone gland.

slides.heading: Hormones of pregnancy
slides.body_md: During pregnancy, several hormone levels rise in the mother’s blood. They support the growth of the foetus, changes in the mother’s metabolism, and the maintenance of pregnancy.

rows: Levels also rise in the mother’s blood

visual.alt: Table of pregnancy hormones with their sources

slides.narration: Two hormones, human chorionic gonadotropin and human placental lactogen, are made only during pregnancy, by the placenta. Their presence is the basis of pregnancy tests. Estrogens and progestogens keep the pregnancy going. Relaxin, from the ovary late in pregnancy, helps prepare for birth, and several other maternal hormones also rise.

slides.heading: Germ layers and stem cells
slides.body_md: Soon after implantation, the inner cell mass differentiates into three **germ layers**: an outer **ectoderm**, a middle **mesoderm** and an inner **endoderm**. All tissues and organs of adults arise from these. Cells of the inner cell mass are **stem cells**, with the potential to give rise to all tissues and organs.

visual.alt: Flow from the inner cell mass to three germ layers, which form all tissues and organs

slides.narration: Every tissue in your body, from skin to bone to the lining of the gut, can be traced back to one of three germ layers formed in the first weeks. The inner cell mass cells that produce them are stem cells, able to become any tissue. That is why stem cells are so important in medical research.

slides.heading: Growth of the foetus
slides.body_md: Human pregnancy lasts about **9 months**. Milestones are usually counted from the start of pregnancy.

rows: Heart has formed; its sound can be heard with a stethoscope
Most major organ systems formed; limbs and external genital organs well developed
First movements felt; hair appears on the head
Body covered with fine hair; eyelids separate; eyelashes formed
Foetus fully developed and ready for delivery

visual.alt: Table of milestones of foetal development from the first to the ninth month

slides.narration: Here is the timeline. By the end of the first month the heart has formed. By the end of the second month the limbs and fingers are developing. By twelve weeks most organ systems are in place. Movements are usually felt in the fifth month. By twenty-four weeks the eyelids have separated. At about nine months the baby is ready to be born.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: is the sample fertile?
slides.body_md: For normal fertility, a semen sample should have at least 60 percent sperms of normal shape and size, and at least 40 percent with vigorous motility. A sample has 250 million sperms. How many must be normal in shape, and how many must swim vigorously, at the minimum?
bullets: Step 1 — Normal shape: $250 \times \dfrac{60}{100} = 150$ million.
Step 2 — Vigorous motility: $250 \times \dfrac{40}{100} = 100$ million.
Step 3 — Why so many? Only a tiny fraction of sperms ever reach the ampulla, and only one fertilises the oocyte.

visual.alt: Worked table: of 250 million sperms, at least 150 million normal and 100 million vigorously motile

slides.narration: A typical ejaculate releases two hundred to three hundred million sperms. Take two hundred and fifty million. Sixty percent of that is one hundred and fifty million sperms of normal shape, and forty percent is one hundred million vigorous swimmers. Such large numbers are needed because most sperms never reach the oviduct.

slides.heading: Parturition: birth
slides.body_md: **Parturition** is induced by a complex **neuroendocrine** mechanism. Signals from the fully developed foetus and the placenta set off mild uterine contractions: the **foetal ejection reflex**.

nodes.label: Oxytocin released by the mother’s pituitary
Baby expelled through the birth canal

visual.alt: Flow of parturition: foetal ejection reflex, oxytocin, stronger contractions in a loop, then delivery of the baby and placenta

slides.narration: Birth is controlled by a loop. The mature foetus and the placenta send signals that cause mild contractions. These trigger the release of oxytocin from the mother’s pituitary. Oxytocin makes the uterine muscle contract harder, which releases still more oxytocin. The loop continues until the baby is pushed out, followed by the placenta.

slides.heading: Lactation
slides.body_md: The **mammary glands** change during pregnancy and start producing milk towards the end of pregnancy: **lactation**. The milk produced in the first few days is **colostrum**.

rows: Contains several antibodies, such as IgA
Gives the newborn ready-made protection against infection
Supports healthy growth; doctors recommend breastfeeding in the first months

visual.alt: Table of colostrum and later breast milk with features and benefits

slides.narration: The very first milk, colostrum, looks thick and yellowish and is especially valuable. It carries antibodies that protect the newborn, whose own immune system is not yet ready. This is why doctors strongly encourage breastfeeding from the first day, and through the early months, for a healthy baby.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Fertilisation in the ampulla; zona pellucida blocks other sperms; meiosis II completes; diploid zygote.
Sex decided by the sperm: X-sperm → girl (XX), Y-sperm → boy (XY); each pregnancy 1/2.
Cleavage → blastomeres → morula (8–16 cells) → blastocyst (trophoblast + inner cell mass) → implantation in the endometrium.
Placenta: chorionic villi + uterine tissue; exchange of gases, food, wastes; hCG, hPL, estrogens, progestogens.
Germ layers from the inner cell mass; about 9 months of gestation.
Parturition: foetal ejection reflex → oxytocin → stronger contractions (positive feedback). Lactation: colostrum with antibodies.

rows: Isthmus, on the way to the uterus

visual.alt: Summary table of where each stage of development takes place

slides.narration: To recap: fertilisation in the ampulla gives a zygote whose sex is decided by the sperm. Cleavage produces a morula and a blastocyst, which implants in the endometrium. The placenta links mother and baby and makes hormones. After about nine months, a positive feedback loop of oxytocin drives birth, and colostrum gives the newborn its first protection.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: State that the **father’s sperm** determines the sex of the baby; explain with XX and XY.
Name **trophoblast** and **inner cell mass** and their fates.
List placental hormones correctly: **hCG, hPL, estrogens, progestogens**; relaxin comes from the **ovary**.
Describe the **foetal ejection reflex** and call the oxytocin loop **positive feedback**.
Name **colostrum** and give its benefit (antibodies such as IgA).
slides.narration: Final tips. In sex determination answers, show the X and Y sperms clearly. Give the fate of both parts of the blastocyst. Do not list relaxin as a placental hormone in this syllabus; it comes from the ovary. And describe birth as a positive feedback loop driven by oxytocin.

notes.title: Human Reproduction — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Overview and the male reproductive system
sections.body_md:
Humans reproduce sexually and are **viviparous**. Events: **gametogenesis → insemination → fertilisation → implantation → gestation → parturition**. Reproductive events begin at puberty; sperm formation continues into old age, while ovum formation stops at about 50 years.

**Testes:** a pair, in the **scrotum**, which keeps them about **2–2.5 °C below** body temperature, as needed for spermatogenesis. Each testis has about **250 testicular lobules**, each with **1–3 seminiferous tubules** lined by **spermatogonia** (male germ cells) and **Sertoli cells** (nourish germ cells). **Interstitial (Leydig) cells** outside the tubules secrete **androgens**; immunologically competent cells are also present there.

**Ducts:** seminiferous tubules → **rete testis** → **vasa efferentia** → **epididymis** → **vas deferens** → (joined by the duct of the seminal vesicle) **ejaculatory duct** → **urethra** → **urethral meatus**.

**Accessory glands:** paired **seminal vesicles**, a **prostate** and paired **bulbourethral glands**. Their secretions form **seminal plasma**, rich in **fructose, calcium and enzymes**; bulbourethral secretions also help lubricate the penis. **Semen** = sperms + seminal plasma.

**External genitalia:** the **penis**, with an enlarged tip, the glans penis, covered by the foreskin.

sections.heading: 2. The female reproductive system and mammary glands
sections.body_md:
**Ovaries:** primary female sex organs (about 2–4 cm long), producing the **ovum** and **ovarian hormones**; each is covered by a thin epithelium enclosing the **ovarian stroma**, with an outer **cortex** and inner **medulla**.

**Oviduct (fallopian tube),** about 10–12 cm: **infundibulum** (funnel near the ovary, with finger-like **fimbriae** that collect the ovum after ovulation) → **ampulla** (wider) → **isthmus** (narrow, joins the uterus).

**Uterus (womb):** single, inverted-pear shape, held by ligaments. Wall: **perimetrium** (outer membrane), **myometrium** (thick smooth muscle; strong contractions at delivery), **endometrium** (inner glandular layer; cyclical changes). The **cervix** opens into the **vagina**; the cervical canal and vagina form the **birth canal**.

**External genitalia:** mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, hymen and clitoris. The hymen can be torn by many everyday activities, so its presence or absence is **not** a reliable indicator of anything.

**Mammary glands:** paired; glandular tissue and fat. Each has **15–20 mammary lobes** with clusters of **alveoli** that secrete milk. Milk path: alveoli → **mammary tubules** → **mammary duct** → **mammary ampulla** → **lactiferous duct**.

sections.heading: 3. Spermatogenesis and the sperm
sections.body_md:
Spermatogenesis begins at **puberty**. **Spermatogonia** (2n = 46) multiply by mitosis; some become **primary spermatocytes** (46), which complete **meiosis I** to form two **secondary spermatocytes** (23 each). **Meiosis II** gives four haploid **spermatids**, which are transformed into **spermatozoa** (**spermiogenesis**). Sperm heads stay embedded in Sertoli cells until they are released from the tubules (**spermiation**).

**Hormonal control:** at puberty the hypothalamus increases **GnRH** → anterior pituitary releases **LH** and **FSH**. **LH → Leydig cells** → androgens, which stimulate spermatogenesis. **FSH → Sertoli cells** → factors that help spermiogenesis.

**Sperm:** head (haploid **nucleus** and cap-like **acrosome** with enzymes for fertilisation), **neck**, **middle piece** (many **mitochondria** for energy) and **tail** (motility); covered by a plasma membrane. A human male ejaculates about **200–300 million** sperms; for normal fertility at least **60 percent** should have normal shape and size and at least **40 percent** vigorous motility.

key_terms.definition_md: Transformation of spermatids into sperms.
Release of sperms from the seminiferous tubules.

sections.heading: 4. Oogenesis and follicles
sections.body_md:
Oogenesis starts during **embryonic development**: millions of **oogonia** form in each foetal ovary, and **none are added after birth**. They begin meiosis and stop at prophase I as **primary oocytes**, each surrounded by granulosa cells as a **primary follicle**. Many follicles degenerate from birth to puberty; about **60,000–80,000** remain in each ovary at puberty.

Primary follicle → **secondary follicle** (more granulosa layers + a new theca) → **tertiary follicle** (fluid-filled **antrum**; theca differentiates into theca interna and theca externa). In the tertiary follicle the primary oocyte completes meiosis I by an **unequal** division: a large haploid **secondary oocyte** and a tiny **first polar body**. The tertiary follicle matures into a **Graafian follicle**; the secondary oocyte forms a new membrane, the **zona pellucida**. The Graafian follicle ruptures to release the secondary oocyte (**ovulation**). Meiosis II is completed only after a sperm enters, giving the ovum and a second polar body.

| Feature | Spermatogenesis | Oogenesis |
|---|---|---|
| Starts | Puberty | Before birth |
| Output per meiocyte | 4 sperms | 1 ovum + polar bodies |
| Cytoplasm division | Equal | Unequal |
| Continues | Into old age | Until menopause (about 50 years) |

sections.heading: 5. The menstrual cycle
sections.body_md:
The reproductive cycle of female primates (monkeys, apes, humans) is the **menstrual cycle**. The first menstruation at puberty is **menarche**; cycles repeat about every **28/29 days** and cease at about 50 years (**menopause**). Usually one ovum is released in the middle of each cycle.

| Phase | Days (28-day) | Events | Hormones |
|---|---|---|---|
| Menstrual | 3–5 days | Endometrium and blood vessels break down and flow out | Progesterone has fallen |
| Follicular (proliferative) | to about day 13 | Primary follicles grow into a Graafian follicle; endometrium regenerates | LH, FSH rise; estrogen from follicles |
| Ovulation | about day 14 | Graafian follicle ruptures | **LH surge** (peak of LH and FSH) |
| Luteal (secretory) | 15–28 | Ruptured follicle → **corpus luteum**; endometrium maintained | **Progesterone** high |

If there is **no fertilisation**, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls and menstruation follows. If **fertilisation** occurs, the corpus luteum is maintained and menstruation does not occur. Lack of menstruation may indicate pregnancy, but it can also be caused by stress or poor health. Menstrual hygiene matters: use clean sanitary products, change them regularly and dispose of them properly.

sections.heading: 6. Fertilisation, cleavage and implantation
sections.body_md:
During insemination, sperms are released into the vagina; motile sperms pass through the cervix and uterus to the oviduct. **Fertilisation** occurs in the **ampullary region** of the oviduct, only if the ovum and sperms reach it together. A sperm's contact with the **zona pellucida** changes the membrane and **blocks other sperms**. Sperm entry makes the secondary oocyte complete **meiosis II** (ovum + second polar body); the haploid nuclei fuse to form a diploid **zygote**.

**Sex determination:** woman XX, man XY; all ova carry X; half the sperms carry X and half Y. X-sperm → **female (XX)**; Y-sperm → **male (XY)**. The sex of the baby is decided by the **father's sperm**.

**Cleavage:** mitotic divisions as the zygote moves through the isthmus → 2, 4, 8, 16 **blastomeres**; 8–16 blastomeres = **morula** → **blastocyst** (outer **trophoblast**, inner cell mass). The trophoblast attaches to the **endometrium**; uterine cells cover the blastocyst: **implantation**. The **inner cell mass** forms the **embryo**.

sections.heading: 7. Pregnancy, placenta, parturition and lactation
sections.body_md:
**Placenta:** chorionic villi from the trophoblast interdigitate with uterine tissue. It supplies **oxygen and nutrients**, removes **carbon dioxide and wastes**, and is connected to the embryo by the **umbilical cord**. It is also an endocrine tissue making **hCG, hPL, estrogens and progestogens**. Late in pregnancy the **ovary** secretes **relaxin**. Estrogens, progestogens, cortisol, prolactin and thyroxine rise in the mother's blood.

**Germ layers:** the inner cell mass forms **ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm**, which give rise to all adult tissues and organs. Inner cell mass cells are **stem cells**.

**Development (about 9 months):** heart by the end of month 1; limbs and digits by the end of month 2; most major organ systems by 12 weeks; first movements and head hair in month 5; fine body hair, separated eyelids and eyelashes by 24 weeks; fully developed by 9 months.

**Parturition:** signals from the fully developed foetus and placenta → mild uterine contractions (**foetal ejection reflex**) → **oxytocin** from the maternal pituitary → stronger contractions → more oxytocin (**positive feedback**) → baby, then placenta, expelled.

**Lactation:** mammary glands produce milk towards the end of pregnancy. **Colostrum**, the milk of the first few days, contains antibodies such as **IgA**, which protect the newborn; breastfeeding is recommended for healthy growth.

key_terms.definition_md: Structural and functional link between embryo and mother formed by chorionic villi and uterine tissue.
Mild uterine contractions triggered by signals from the mature foetus and placenta that start parturition.
First milk after birth, rich in antibodies.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that fertilisation occurs in the uterus (it occurs in the ampulla of the oviduct).
- Saying the mature ovum is released at ovulation (it is the **secondary oocyte**).
- Giving 46 chromosomes for a secondary spermatocyte (it has 23).
- Saying oogenesis begins at puberty (it begins before birth).
- Listing relaxin as a placental hormone (here it is secreted by the ovary in late pregnancy).
- Saying the mother determines the sex of the child.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: term, location, chromosome number or hormone.
- 2–3-mark answers: correct sequence or structure (1) + function or reason (1) + example, number or labelled sketch (1).
- 5-mark answers: labelled diagram (male or female system, seminiferous tubule, sperm, ovary, blastocyst) (2) + process in order (2) + one significance point (1).
- Case-based items: two 1-mark parts and a 2-mark part with an internal choice, often reading a cycle chart or a set of numbers.

questions.stem_md: Which sequence shows the correct path of sperms from the testis to the outside?

options.text_md: Vasa efferentia → rete testis → epididymis → vas deferens → urethra → ejaculatory duct
Rete testis → epididymis → vasa efferentia → ejaculatory duct → vas deferens → urethra
Epididymis → rete testis → vas deferens → vasa efferentia → urethra → ejaculatory duct
Rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra

questions.solution_md: From the seminiferous tubules, sperms pass through the rete testis, vasa efferentia, epididymis and vas deferens, then the ejaculatory duct into the urethra — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which layer of the uterine wall produces strong contractions during the delivery of a baby?
questions.solution_md: The myometrium is the thick middle layer of smooth muscle that contracts strongly during delivery — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the mammary gland, milk is secreted by the cells of the
questions.solution_md: Clusters of cells called alveoli secrete milk, which then flows through tubules, ducts and the ampulla to the lactiferous duct — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a boy, one testis fails to descend into the scrotum and remains inside the abdomen. If this is not corrected, what is most likely to happen to that testis after puberty?

options.text_md: It will produce more sperms, because it is better protected.
It will produce few or no sperms, because the abdomen is warmer than the scrotum.
It will stop making androgens but produce normal sperms.
It will produce ova instead of sperms.

questions.solution_md: Spermatogenesis needs a temperature about 2–2.5 °C below body temperature, which the scrotum provides. Inside the abdomen the testis is too warm, so sperm production fails — option (b).

questions.stem_md: If both vasa deferentia of a man are blocked, which of these would his semen most likely contain?

options.text_md: Sperms and seminal plasma, as before

questions.solution_md: Sperms reach the ejaculatory duct only through the vas deferens, but the seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands open beyond the block. So the fluid part is still released without sperms — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A semen sample has normal numbers of sperms, but they soon stop moving, and the seminal plasma is found to lack fructose. A problem in which glands is most likely?
questions.solution_md: Fructose in seminal plasma comes mainly from the seminal vesicles and is the energy source for sperm movement — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Leydig cells are found inside the seminiferous tubules, between the spermatogonia.

**Reason (R):** Leydig cells secrete androgens.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: Leydig (interstitial) cells lie in the spaces outside the seminiferous tubules; Sertoli cells are the ones inside. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Match each part of the oviduct (column I) with its description (column II).

match_right.text_md: Finger-like projections that help collect the ovum
Narrow part that joins the uterus
Wider part where fertilisation usually occurs
Funnel-shaped part closest to the ovary

questions.solution_md: Infundibulum = funnel near the ovary; fimbriae = finger-like edges that collect the ovum; ampulla = wider part (site of fertilisation); isthmus = narrow part joining the uterus.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In humans, fertilisation normally takes place in the uterus.
questions.solution_md: False. Fertilisation normally takes place in the ampullary region of the oviduct; the embryo implants in the uterus later.

questions.stem_md: Each human testis has about 250 lobules, each with one to three seminiferous tubules. What is the greatest number of seminiferous tubules that the two testes of a man could contain?
questions.solution_md: Most per testis $= 250 \times 3 = 750$; two testes $= 2 \times 750 = 1500$.

questions.stem_md: The cervical canal together with the vagina forms the ______.
questions.solution_md: Birth canal.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between Sertoli cells and Leydig cells on the basis of their location and function.

answer.model_answer_md: **Sertoli cells** lie **inside** the seminiferous tubules, among the germ cells; they **nourish** the developing germ cells. **Leydig (interstitial) cells** lie **outside** the tubules, in the interstitial spaces; they **secrete androgens** such as testosterone.

questions.solution_md: Compare location (inside vs outside the tubules) and function (nourishment vs androgen secretion).

questions.stem_md: Hospitals advise surgery for a baby boy whose testes have not descended into the scrotum. Explain the biological reason for this advice.

answer.model_answer_md: Sperm formation needs a temperature about **2–2.5 °C lower** than normal body temperature. The scrotum keeps the testes outside the abdomen at this lower temperature. Testes left in the warmer abdomen cannot carry out normal **spermatogenesis**, so the man could later be infertile.

questions.solution_md: Link the scrotal temperature to spermatogenesis.

marking_scheme.step: Spermatogenesis needs a lower temperature, given by the scrotum
Undescended testes are too warm, so sperm formation fails

questions.stem_md: Trace the path of milk from where it is made in the mammary gland to where the baby sucks it out.

answer.model_answer_md: Milk is secreted by the cells of the **alveoli** in the mammary lobes and stored in their cavities. It flows through **mammary tubules** into a **mammary duct**; several ducts join to form a wider **mammary ampulla**, which is connected to the **lactiferous duct** through which the baby sucks milk.

questions.solution_md: Alveoli → tubules → duct → ampulla → lactiferous duct.

marking_scheme.step: Tubules → duct → ampulla → lactiferous duct, in order

questions.stem_md: Name the three layers of the uterine wall from outside to inside and give one role of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Perimetrium:** the thin outer membrane that covers the uterus.

2. **Myometrium:** the thick middle layer of smooth muscle, which contracts strongly to push the baby out during delivery.

3. **Endometrium:** the inner glandular lining, which thickens and breaks down in each menstrual cycle and in which the embryo implants.

questions.solution_md: Perimetrium (covering), myometrium (contractions), endometrium (cyclical lining, implantation).

questions.stem_md: Draw a labelled diagram of the human male reproductive system (front view). Describe the roles of the testes and of the three kinds of accessory glands.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Diagram labels:** testis, scrotum, epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle, ejaculatory duct, prostate, bulbourethral gland, urinary bladder, urethra, penis, urethral meatus.

**Testes.** They lie in the scrotum, which keeps them about 2–2.5 °C below body temperature. Their seminiferous tubules produce sperms, with Sertoli cells nourishing the germ cells; the Leydig cells between the tubules secrete androgens.

**Seminal vesicles (a pair)** and the **prostate** add most of the seminal plasma, which is rich in fructose, calcium and enzymes; fructose provides energy for sperm movement.

**Bulbourethral glands (a pair)** add a secretion that helps lubricate the penis.

Sperms together with seminal plasma form semen, which leaves through the urethra.

questions.solution_md: Labelled diagram, then testes (sperms and androgens) and the three glands (seminal plasma, lubrication).

Role of testes: sperms (Sertoli) and androgens (Leydig)
Seminal vesicles and prostate: seminal plasma with fructose, calcium, enzymes

questions.stem_md: How many chromosomes does a human secondary spermatocyte have?
questions.solution_md: The secondary spermatocyte forms after meiosis I, which halves the number from 46 to 23 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: When are the oogonia of a woman formed?
questions.solution_md: Millions of oogonia form in each foetal ovary, and no more are formed after birth — option (d).

questions.stem_md: If 120 primary spermatocytes in a testis complete spermatogenesis, how many sperms will be formed?
questions.solution_md: Each primary spermatocyte gives 4 spermatids, each becoming one sperm: $120 \times 4 = 480$.

questions.stem_md: Thirty primary spermatocytes and thirty primary oocytes complete gametogenesis (the oocytes after sperm entry). How many more functional gametes are formed from the spermatocytes than from the oocytes?
questions.solution_md: Sperms $= 30 \times 4 = 120$; ova $= 30 \times 1 = 30$ (the other products are polar bodies). Difference $= 120 - 30 = 90$.

questions.stem_md: Which cell is released from the Graafian follicle at ovulation in humans?
questions.solution_md: The primary oocyte completes meiosis I inside the tertiary follicle; the Graafian follicle then releases the secondary oocyte, which completes meiosis II only after a sperm enters — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A drug blocks the receptors for LH on the Leydig cells of an adult male. Which change is expected first?

options.text_md: FSH stops acting on Sertoli cells, so spermiation increases.
The seminiferous tubules start producing ova.
Androgen secretion falls, so spermatogenesis is reduced.
Androgen secretion rises, so more sperms are made.

questions.stem_md: Describe spermatogenesis in humans with a flow chart showing the chromosome number at each stage. How is the process controlled by hormones?

answer.model_answer_md:
**Flow chart:** spermatogonium (46) → primary spermatocyte (46) → meiosis I → two secondary spermatocytes (23 each) → meiosis II → four spermatids (23 each) → spermiogenesis → four sperms (23 each).

**Process.** Spermatogenesis begins at puberty in the seminiferous tubules. Spermatogonia on the inner wall multiply by mitosis, and some enlarge into primary spermatocytes. Each completes the first meiotic division to form two haploid secondary spermatocytes, which complete the second division to form four spermatids. The spermatids are transformed into sperms (spermiogenesis), and the sperms are finally released from the tubules (spermiation).

**Hormonal control.** At puberty, the hypothalamus increases GnRH, which makes the anterior pituitary release LH and FSH. LH acts on the Leydig cells, which secrete androgens that stimulate spermatogenesis. FSH acts on the Sertoli cells and stimulates factors that help spermiogenesis.

marking_scheme.step: Flow chart with correct chromosome numbers

questions.stem_md: Describe oogenesis in humans, including the stages of follicle development, up to ovulation and fertilisation. Show the main steps in a flow chart.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Flow chart:** oogonium (46) → primary oocyte (46, arrested in prophase I) → [in tertiary follicle] meiosis I → secondary oocyte (23) + first polar body → ovulation → [after sperm entry] meiosis II → ovum (23) + second polar body.

**Before birth.** Millions of oogonia form in each foetal ovary; none are added later. They enter meiosis I and stop at prophase as primary oocytes, each surrounded by granulosa cells in a primary follicle. Many degenerate before puberty.

**After puberty.** Primary follicles gain layers of granulosa cells and a theca (secondary follicles), then a fluid-filled antrum (tertiary follicles). In the tertiary follicle, the primary oocyte completes meiosis I unequally, forming a large secondary oocyte and a tiny polar body. The follicle matures into a Graafian follicle; the oocyte forms the zona pellucida. The Graafian follicle ruptures to release the secondary oocyte (ovulation), which completes meiosis II only when a sperm enters.

questions.solution_md: Before birth (oogonia, primary oocytes, primary follicles), after puberty (follicle stages, unequal meiosis I, Graafian follicle, ovulation), meiosis II at fertilisation.

marking_scheme.step: Flow chart with polar bodies and chromosome numbers

Ovulation of the secondary oocyte; meiosis II after sperm entry

questions.stem_md: State the role of each of the following in the menstrual cycle: (a) estrogen, (b) LH, (c) progesterone.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Estrogen**, secreted by the growing follicles in the follicular phase, makes the endometrium **regenerate** (proliferate).

(b) **LH** from the anterior pituitary reaches a peak at mid-cycle; this **LH surge** causes **ovulation**, the rupture of the Graafian follicle, and the formation of the corpus luteum.

(c) **Progesterone**, secreted by the corpus luteum in the luteal phase, **maintains the endometrium** for implantation.

questions.solution_md: Estrogen regenerates, LH surge causes ovulation, progesterone maintains.

questions.stem_md: Describe the events of the ovary and the uterus in the four phases of a 28-day menstrual cycle, naming the hormones that control them. What happens if the ovum is fertilised?

answer.model_answer_md:
**Menstrual phase (about days 1–5).** The endometrium and its blood vessels break down and flow out as menstrual flow, because progesterone has fallen after the corpus luteum degenerated.

**Follicular (proliferative) phase.** Pituitary LH and FSH rise gradually; primary follicles grow into a mature Graafian follicle. Estrogen from the growing follicles makes the endometrium regenerate.

**Ovulation (about day 14).** LH and FSH reach a peak; the LH surge ruptures the Graafian follicle, which releases the secondary oocyte.

**Luteal (secretory) phase.** The ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes large amounts of progesterone that maintain the endometrium for implantation. Without fertilisation, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls and a new menstrual phase starts.

**If fertilised,** the corpus luteum is maintained, the endometrium is kept for the embryo and menstruation stops during pregnancy.

questions.solution_md: Four phases with ovarian and uterine events and LH, FSH, estrogen and progesterone; pregnancy keeps the corpus luteum.

marking_scheme.step: Follicular phase: follicle growth, estrogen, endometrium regeneration
If fertilised: corpus luteum maintained, no menstruation

(b) Fertilisation normally occurs in the **ampullary region** of the oviduct, beyond the isthmus.

(c) **Yes.** The ovaries and pituitary still work, so follicles grow, ovulation occurs and, without pregnancy, the corpus luteum degenerates and menstruation follows each cycle.

questions.stem_md: Using a simple chart of sex chromosomes, explain why it is the father and not the mother who determines whether a baby is a boy or a girl.

answer.model_answer_md:
Mother **XX** → all ova carry **X**. Father **XY** → half the sperms carry **X** and half carry **Y**.

- Ovum (X) + X-sperm → **XX** → girl.
- Ovum (X) + Y-sperm → **XY** → boy.

Since the mother always contributes an X, the sex depends on **which kind of sperm** fertilises the ovum, so it is decided by the father; each pregnancy has an equal chance of a boy or a girl.

questions.solution_md: Chart of XX and XY gametes and the two fertilisations.

questions.stem_md: Describe the events from insemination to the implantation of the embryo in humans.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Insemination and transport.** Sperms released into the vagina swim through the cervix and uterus to the oviduct. The secondary oocyte released at ovulation is collected by the fimbriae and moves into the oviduct.

**Fertilisation.** It occurs only if the oocyte and sperms reach the ampullary region together. When a sperm contacts the zona pellucida, changes in the membrane block other sperms. The sperm’s entry makes the secondary oocyte complete meiosis II, forming the ovum and a second polar body; the haploid nuclei fuse to form a diploid zygote.

**Cleavage.** As the zygote moves through the isthmus towards the uterus, it divides by mitosis into 2, 4, 8 and 16 blastomeres; with 8–16 blastomeres it is a morula, which develops into a blastocyst.

**Implantation.** The blastocyst’s outer trophoblast attaches to the endometrium; the uterine cells cover it and it becomes embedded. The inner cell mass develops into the embryo.

questions.solution_md: Transport → fertilisation in the ampulla (block to other sperms, meiosis II) → cleavage, morula, blastocyst → implantation.

marking_scheme.step: Fertilisation in the ampulla with the block to other sperms
Completion of meiosis II and zygote formation
Implantation: trophoblast attaches, inner cell mass forms the embryo

questions.stem_md: In a village, a woman who has given birth to three daughters is blamed by her relatives for “not giving them a son”. Evaluate this belief using your knowledge of sex determination, and suggest how a health worker could respond.

answer.model_answer_md:
**The science.** The mother is XX, so every ovum she produces carries an X chromosome. The father is XY, so half his sperms carry X and half carry Y. A girl results when an X-bearing sperm fertilises the ovum, and a boy when a Y-bearing sperm does. The sex of the baby is therefore decided by the father’s sperm, by chance, and not by the mother.

**Chance.** In every pregnancy the chance of a girl is about one half. Three girls in a row has a probability of one eighth, so it happens in many families and does not indicate any fault in either parent.

**Evaluation.** The belief is scientifically wrong and unfair; it harms the mother’s health and dignity and can lead to pressure for sex selection, which is illegal in India.

**Response.** The health worker could explain the X and Y sperm chart simply, stress that daughters and sons are equally valuable, and support the mother’s health.

questions.solution_md: XX and XY gametes; sperm decides; probability 1/8; belief is wrong and harmful; respectful explanation.

marking_scheme.step: Gametes of mother and father correctly stated

Sensible response by the health worker

Researchers describe the usual timetable of a human embryo in its first week.

| Days after fertilisation | Where | What is seen |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ampulla of the oviduct | Zygote, then 2 cells |
| 3 | Isthmus | A solid ball of about 12 cells |
